_about: The economy (PRD, "M4 Economy", "Eminent domain" and "Prices in 2026 dollars"; M4-01). Every number M4 runs on, read by the issues after M4-01. Money is whole dollars. A price is an `amount` in whole dollars of its `sourceYear`, with a `source`, and `index` says how it is raised to 2026: `construction` by the highway construction index in roads.json, `general` by `generalEscalation` here, since property values, relocation payments, charges and grants are not construction. A figure with no usable source says `placeholder: true`, and its `source` says what it stands in for. Shares and rates are fractions, 0.01 for one percent, and each says where it came from the same way. `taxRates` are the four sliders' defaults and ranges: residential is a yearly rate on property value, commercial a rate on sales, office and industrial a rate on output, and mixed pays the residential and commercial rates (M4.md). `developmentCharges` are dollars per square metre of floor space a new building adds, a default and a range for each of the five zones: mixed has its own, since a mixed building is one project (M4-08). A new building pays its zone's rate times its floor space, and a redevelopment pays it on the floor space it adds over the buildings it replaces. `developmentChargeGrowth.shareAtMax` is how much of a zone's daily building quota is left with its charge at the top of its range: the share falls in a straight line from 1 at a charge of 0, multiplies the zone's want, at least one a day while its bar is above zero, before it is rounded, and the fraction left over is built on that share of days. `business` is what a shop sells and an office or factory makes a year for each job filled, the base the commercial, office and industrial rates are charged on (M4-06); mixed pays the commercial rate on all its jobs, its offices' output included. A building's value (`value`, economy/value.ts) is its floor space by use times that use's dollars per square metre, times a land value factor: `1 - landValueWeight + landValueWeight × landValue / landValueReference`, so at the reference land value a square metre is worth its price, and the weight is the share of the price that follows the land. Floor space follows room and jobs, not lot area: `perResident` square metres for each resident a building holds room for, and `perJob` for each job by kind, so a mixed building adds its homes and its shops. `eminentDomain` prices clearing an occupied building: its value, plus `relocationPerResident` for each resident and `relocationPerJob` for each job it holds room for, plus `premium.share` times the value. A vacant or abandoned building costs `demolitionPerSquareMetre` of its floor space only. A building is occupied while somebody lives or works in it, and the relocation payments count the residents and the jobs filled that clearing it displaces. Clearing something the city owns costs its demolition less `refundShare.share` of its build cost. `expropriationRecords.max` is the most expropriation records state keeps (M4-09): one for each occupied building cleared by the city, each kept a game year. `loans` are what the city may borrow: at most `maxOpen` at once, each on one of `offers`. The credit limit is `perResident` dollars for each resident plus `lastYearTaxMultiple` times the tax income of the last twelve months in the history, times `largerLoansMultiple` once the city has opened `largerLoans` (M4-11). It bounds what the open loans owe together. `generalEscalation` is one year of the consumer price index, the 12 months to September 2026, applied to every year before 2026 as roads.json's index is; that is a stand-in for the years before, which only matters for prices more than a year old. Every number here is a starting value; M4-19 tuned the tax rates and priced the other city spending. `otherSpending.perResident` is what the city spends a year for each resident on the services that have no building yet (M4-19), charged a day at a time with the upkeep. `landmarks` lists the city's unique buildings (M4-13, PRD "Landmarks"). A landmark's place in the list is its type in saves, so append new ones and never reorder. Each names the unlock that opens it (progression.json), its lot in cells along and back from the road, its price, the floor space its demolition is priced on, and its yearly upkeep as a share of its price.

generalEscalation.source: US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index news release of 14 October 2026: the all items index rose 3.7 percent over the 12 months to September 2026.

startingGrant.source: Placeholder. Enough for about 10 km of street at the 2026 street price, so a first town can be laid out before any tax comes in (PRD, "One thing to watch is the early game").

overdraft.source: Placeholder. How far below zero the treasury may fall (PRD: "a small overdraft").

residential.source: Placeholder. A yearly rate on property value. US effective property tax rates sit near one percent of home value; no single source was read. Tuned in M4-19: the game's taxes stand in for everything a real city takes in, transfers from higher governments and fees included, so its rates sit about 1.65 to 1.8 times what US cities levy, and the budget per resident comes out near Toronto's (otherSpending). At these defaults a compact density 1 town of houses with shops and offices nets about zero a year after its roads and its other spending, and the same people on cul-de-sacs lose money (test/economy-scenarios.test.ts). The top of the range is about three times the default, as before.

commercial.source: Placeholder. A rate on sales; a US city or county adds about two percent to the state sales tax, no single source read. Tuned in M4-19: the game's taxes stand in for everything a real city takes in, transfers from higher governments and fees included, so its rates sit about 1.65 to 1.8 times what US cities levy, and the budget per resident comes out near Toronto's (otherSpending). At these defaults a compact density 1 town of houses with shops and offices nets about zero a year after its roads and its other spending, and the same people on cul-de-sacs lose money (test/economy-scenarios.test.ts). The top of the range is about three times the default, as before.

residential.source: Placeholder. Dollars per square metre of floor space added; a 200 square metre house pays $20,000. No source read for North American charges per square metre.

commercial.source: Placeholder. Dollars per square metre of floor space added.

office.source: Placeholder. Dollars per square metre of floor space added.

industrial.source: Placeholder. Dollars per square metre of floor space added, lower than shops and offices since factories cover more ground for each job.

mixed.source: Placeholder. Dollars per square metre of floor space added, at the residential figure since most of a mixed building's floor space is homes.

developmentChargeGrowth.source: Placeholder. The share of a zone's daily building quota left with its development charge at the top of its range; the share falls in a straight line from 1 at a charge of 0. No source read for how charges slow construction.

salesPerJob.source: US Census Bureau, Annual Retail Trade Survey: US retail sales (NAICS 44-45) of $7,041.0 billion in 2022, over about 15.6 million retail jobs, $451,000 a job.
salesPerJob.note: The sales total has a source; the job count is the BLS retail trade figure for 2022 from memory, not a source read.

office.source: Placeholder. A rate on output, which no real city levies, so the output is set to an office job's value: 56 square metres at $1,870, so an office pays at its rate about what a home of the same floor space pays at the residential rate. The 2025 price per square metre makes it a 2025 figure. Worked out by hand, so it does not follow either number if they change.

industrial.source: Placeholder. US manufacturing value added of about $2.9 trillion in 2024 over about 12.9 million manufacturing jobs, from memory of the BEA and BLS figures; no table was read.

business.source: Business tax follows activity (PRD, "M4 Economy"). M4 has no trips or freight, so a shop's sales and an office's or factory's output follow its jobs filled (M4-06): `salesPerJob` dollars a year for each shop job filled, scaled down while the city's shop jobs filled are more than its residents' spending power keeps busy (demand.json), and `outputPerJob` for each office or factory job filled, a factory's only while its road reaches an outside connection. M5 swaps in trips and freight and keeps the rates.

residential.source: US Census Bureau, Characteristics of New Housing, 2025 highlights: median sales price of a new single-family house $417,400, median size 2,194 square feet. $190 a square foot, $2,045 a square metre, land included.
residential.note: A ratio of two medians, not a median of prices per square foot. A sale price, not an assessed value; assessments run below sale prices in many places.

commercial.source: Crexi National CRE Report, September 2025: median sold price of retail property $220.23 a square foot, $2,370 a square metre.
commercial.note: Sales on one listing platform, not assessed values.

office.source: Crexi National CRE Report, September 2025: median sold price of office property $173.71 a square foot, $1,870 a square metre.
office.note: Sales on one listing platform, not assessed values, in a year office prices were low.

industrial.source: Crexi National CRE Report, September 2025: median sold price of industrial property $107.56 a square foot, $1,158 a square metre.
industrial.note: Sales on one listing platform, not assessed values.

value.source: Placeholder. The prices above are national medians, so they are taken to hold at land value 50, a middling lot. Half the price follows land value, about the land's share of US home values in the national accounts; no single source was read.

floorSpace.source: Per resident: the 2025 median new single-family house, 2,194 square feet (US Census Bureau, Characteristics of New Housing), over the four residents a single family home holds room for in buildings.json. Per job: Metropolitan Council, How to Measure Employment Intensity and Capacity: 920 square feet a retail job, 600 an office job and 1,500 a warehouse job.
floorSpace.note: The house size is from 2025. The Metropolitan Council's figures per job carry no year, so the block has no source year.

relocationPerResident.source: FHWA final rule on the Uniform Relocation Act, effective 3 June 2024: the rental assistance payment for a tenant household rose to $9,570, from $7,200. Over the 2.5 people of an average US household, $3,828 a resident.
relocationPerResident.note: The cap has a source; the household size does not. Read from WSDOT's summary of the federal changes, not the rule itself. A homeowner's replacement housing payment is up to $41,200; the tenant figure is taken because most displaced residents in a dense city rent. The cap is a most, and moving costs come on top. The household size is from memory, not a source read.

relocationPerJob.source: FHWA final rule on the Uniform Relocation Act, effective 3 June 2024: reestablishment expenses for a displaced business rose to $33,200. Spread over a placeholder business of ten jobs, $3,320 a job.
relocationPerJob.note: The cap has a source; ten jobs a business does not.

premium.source: Michigan Constitution, Article X, section 2 (2006): a principal residence taken for public use is paid at least 125 percent of its fair market value. Applied to every building, not only homes.

demolitionPerSquareMetre.source: Placeholder. Cost guides put commercial demolition at $4 to $8 a square foot of floor space (HelloData, Average Demolition Cost Per Square Foot in Commercial Real Estate); $6, $65 a square metre. Not a primary source.

refundShare.source: Placeholder. The share of a city-owned road's or building's build cost paid back when it is cleared, for salvage. No source.

expropriationRecords.source: Placeholder. Enough for twenty `BulldozeBuilding` commands at their cap of 1,000 buildings within one game year before the oldest records go early. A record is six numbers and a player id, so the list stays under a few megabytes in a save.

loans.source: Placeholder. Terms of 10, 20 and 30 years, about what US municipal bonds run, at rates a little above high-grade municipal yields; no source read.

perResident.source: Placeholder. Dollars of borrowing for each resident.

creditLimit.source: Placeholder. Borrowing of three years of tax income, and twice the limit once the milestone that opens `largerLoans` in progression.json is reached; no source read.

perResident.source: City of Toronto 2026 operating budget of C$18.9 billion, less the TTC's C$3.03 billion (transit is M6 and M7, with fares and operating costs of its own) and Transportation Services' C$516.0 million (roads, which the road upkeep line charges), over the city's 3.27 million residents: C$4,693 a resident, rounded to $4,700. Dollars are not converted (PRD, "Prices in 2026 dollars").
perResident.note: The TTC figure is the TTC Board's recommended 2026 gross budget (TTC news release, January 2026), the Transportation Services figure its 2026 budget notes' gross expenditures, and the population Statistics Canada's estimate for 1 January 2025 as citypopulation.de reproduces it; none of the three was read in the city's own tables. Chicago's FY2026 budget of $16.6 billion (Civic Federation) over about 2.7 million residents is near $6,100, with water, sewer and the airports in it and the CTA not. What the city spends on each resident falls very little with density, so this line does not tell a suburb from a downtown: roads, and the jobs a district holds, do.

otherSpending.source: The city's spending on what has no building yet, per resident a year (M4.md, "Spending that has no building yet"; M4-19), charged a day at a time on the other spending line with the daily share of the population that day. M8 and M9 replace it a service at a time, each taking off the share its services stand for.

price.source: Huntsville, Alabama's new city hall: an $82.8 million project led by Turner Construction that started in January 2022 (Engineering News-Record, "Huntsville, Ala., Starts New Chapter With $82M City Hall").
price.note: The amount and year are from the article's headline and summary as a search returned them; the article itself was not read. A project total, which may cover more than construction.

floorSpace.source: Placeholder. About 100,000 square feet, a mid-sized city hall; Huntsville's floor area was not read. Its demolition is priced on it.

upkeepShare.source: Placeholder. Two percent of the build cost a year, about what facility maintenance guides budget for a public building; no single source read.
